issues.item: Triggers: Offender Cues: Seeing the offender
issues.explanation: 'Seeing the offender' is difficult to reconcile with a man-made disaster trauma unless the event involved a clearly identifiable perpetrator who remains visually encountered; in this trauma context it is a hard-to-explain trigger compared with the other disaster-linked cues.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Mirror Checking: keep checking mirrors
issues.explanation: 'Keep checking mirrors' suggests a specific interpersonal pursuit/being-followed safety behavior. That strategy is not well supported by the rest of the profile, which centers on disaster-related auditory threat, generalized danger, and avoidance of reminders/unfamiliar places rather than pursuit-based hypervigilance.

'Belong Nowhere' implies a strong social alienation/shame-based appraisal that is not well supported by the rest of the profile, which is otherwise dominated by danger, vigilance, and guilt themes related to man-made disaster exposure. It is not impossible, but here it stands out as thematically disconnected from the other selected items.

'Avoid Unfamiliar Places' is phrased more like an avoidance/behavioral strategy than a threat belief. Within the current profile, threat items otherwise reflect perceived ongoing danger and inability to feel safe; this item is misaligned with the node content and duplicates the avoidance theme already captured under maladaptive strategies.

vignette:
Nia is a 48-year-old rabbi who came to treatment more than a year after a man-made explosion shattered the sense of safety she had once carried so naturally into other people’s fear. She had been attending a community interfaith gathering when there was a sudden blast outside the building, a violent bang that threw people to the floor and sent glass and debris inward. What stayed with her most was not only the sound but the split second in which she froze, trying to understand what was happening while others screamed and pushed toward the exits. Since then, explosion-like sounds have had an immediate force for her: a car backfiring outside the synagogue, a construction bang on the street, even a slammed metal door can pull her back into that moment. News coverage of attacks or public violence has become similarly potent, not as abstract information but as something that makes her body brace as if another blast is already underway.

In the weeks afterward, Nia found that reassurance no longer reached her. Her husband could tell her the neighborhood was quiet, congregants could remind her that security had been improved, and she would still feel certain that safety was fragile, provisional, not to be trusted. That sense becomes sharper after dark. At night she checks locks more than once, listens for unusual sounds, and finds herself alert to the windows in a way she never used to be. In public she scans automatically—who is near the entrance, who is lingering too long, who seems to be watching. Because she feels so continuously on guard, she has come to believe that this vigilance is necessary, that one can never assume things will be fine and that only constant care stands between ordinary life and catastrophe. The same fearful alertness has also darkened her view of the future; when she is keyed up like this, it feels plausible to her that nothing genuinely good lies ahead, only the possibility of the next disaster.

Her work keeps these fears alive in concrete ways. As a rabbi she stands in visible spaces—on the bimah, at hospital bedsides, at community meetings—and being seen now often feels perilous rather than ordinary. If she notices someone lingering at the back of the sanctuary or feels a stranger’s eyes on her after services, she does not experience it as neutral attention; under the pressure of constant threat-monitoring, the feeling of being watched becomes a warning sign. She catches herself searching faces, exits, hands, doorways. News alerts on her phone, especially reports involving bombings or attacks on religious communities, can set off the same state of alarm, not simply because of the content but because she is already primed to detect danger everywhere.

Nia speaks with particular shame about having done “nothing useful” when the explosion happened. She knows, intellectually, that people were confused and terrified, but she has come to judge herself harshly for not having done more to stop what happened or protect others in those first seconds. That guilt has shaped her life in ways that make sense to her from the inside. Because she believes the world can turn without warning and that she failed once by not being prepared enough, she now avoids anything that might leave her feeling exposed or unguarded. She steers away when congregants want to revisit the event with her, changes the subject if others mention it, and refuses invitations to memorial discussions. At home she has withdrawn from sex with her husband, not out of lack of care for him but because physical closeness requires letting go of vigilance, and she feels she cannot afford that. Instead she keeps watch—checking outside before bed, noting every sound in the house, positioning herself to monitor doors and windows.

Over months, these habits have narrowed her world and confirmed the beliefs underneath them. Avoiding reminders has prevented any chance of discovering that speaking about the blast would not make it happen again. Avoiding sex has left her marriage strained and lonely, which she privately reads as further proof that nothing good can happen to her anymore. Her constant checking brings momentary relief, yet it also keeps her attention fixed on danger cues; after an evening spent scanning the street outside the parsonage-like home attached to the synagogue, a bang or a news notification lands with even more force. The more she organizes her life around preventing the next catastrophe, the more she feels that catastrophe is always near, and the more unforgivable her original “inaction” seems to her.

She finally sought help after a recent Friday evening service, when a loud noise from nearby street construction made her visibly flinch mid-prayer. She lost her place, stared toward the back doors, and afterward was shaken by how many congregants had noticed. What frightened her most was not only the reaction itself but the idea that this is now her life: watchful, unreachable by reassurance, unable to imagine ease, and pulling away from the people she loves. She says she wants help because she is tired of living as if the blast is still about to happen, yet part of her is afraid that lowering her guard even slightly would be the very mistake she can never forgive herself for making once already.
